contests.title: Ballot Measure No.2 — 24ESEG - An Act Restoring Political Party Primaries, Ending Ranked-Choice General Elections, and Repealing Recent Campaign Finance Laws

provenance.quote:
Ballot Measure No.2
24ESEG - An Act Restoring
Political Party Primaries,
Ending Ranked-Choice
General Elections, and
Repealing Recent Campaign
Finance Laws
This act would get rid of open primary elections,
where all candidates appear on one ballot. It would
also get rid of ranked-choice general elections. It
would bring back political party primaries and
single-choice general elections. It would also repeal
certain campaign finance rules that were added by
a 2020 ballot measure.
Elections would occur as they did before open
primaries and ranked choice voting. In the primary
election, voters would choose a party’s ballot,
unless prohibited by the party’s bylaws. They would
only vote for candidates on that ballot. The winning
candidate from each primary would be the party’s
nominee. In the general election, voters would vote
for only one candidate in each race. The candidate
with the most votes would win. Party petitions,
special runoff elections, and other processes would
return. Candidates for governor and lieutenant
governor would run separately in political party
primaries and then together in the general election.
This act would also repeal campaign finance rules
that were passed in 2020. It would remove the
limits on donations to joint campaigns for governor
and lieutenant governor. It would remove limits and
disclosure rules under current law, including for
digital ads, out-of-state donations, undisclosed
donations, and the true source of donations. It
would change the meaning of a campaign
expenditure and remove some fines.
Should this initiative become law?

voterGuide.summary:
This Act will reverse changes made by voters in 2020 to state elections.
The Act changes the rules for primary elections. The Act ends the top four open primary. The primary
will be a party primary. The director of elections will make a ballot for each party. Each party ballot will
list the candidates running for that party’s nomination.
The Act changes the campaign finance rules. The Act removes limits on contributions to a joint
campaign for governor and lieutenant governor. The Act allows entities to accept more than $2,000
in dark money. The Act lets people contribute money through a third party without disclosing the true
source. The Act ends a requirement that a “paid for by” message appear during the entirety of a
communication. The Act ends a requirement that a disclaimer appear on ads paid for by an outside
source.

Ballot Measure No. 2 - 24ESEG
An Act Restoring Political Party Primaries, Ending Ranked-Choice
General Elections, and Repealing Recent Campaign Finance Laws
A party will choose who may run and vote in its primary. In the primary a voter may vote only one
party’s ballot. The person who gets the most votes in a party primary is the party’s nominee. The party
nominees will move on to the general election. Other candidates may petition to be on the general
election ballot. Reenacts unconstitutional law that a candidate must register as a member of a political
party to run in that party’s primary. Reenacts unconstitutional laws requiring a separate ballot for each
political party.
The Act changes the process used to fill vacancies in office. The Act ends special primaries. A party will
use a petition to nominate its candidate for a special election to fill a vacancy. Other candidates may
petition to be on the ballot. The Act adds a special runoff to some races. The Act sets the timeframes
for special elections and special runoff elections. The governor will call a special runoff if no candidate
in a special election for congress gets more than half the votes. A ballot measure may appear on a
special runoff ballot. When the governor appoints a person to fill a vacancy in the state legislature, the
governor will appoint a member of the same party, if any, that nominated the predecessor.
The Act changes the ballot for general elections. The ballot will show a candidate’s party designation,
if any. Write-in candidates for governor and lieutenant governor will be members of the same party or
group. The Act changes voting in general elections. The Act ends ranked-choice voting. A voter will
vote for one candidate for each office; the candidate with the most votes wins.
The Act will change the definition of “political party”. Members of the governor’s party and members
of the party that received the second most votes in the last election for governor will serve on some
state boards. The Governor must appoint two members of the Alaska Public Offices Commission
from lists made by these parties. A candidate may appoint a poll watcher if the candidate does not
represent a party.

argumentsFor:
Voting Yes on Ballot Measure 2 restores Alaska’s elections to how they were before 2020:
1. End Ranked Choice Voting
2. Bring Back Open Primaries
3. Restore Pre-2020 Campaign Disclosure Laws
(1) Yes on 2 Ends Ranked Choice Voting
• Dark Money: Out-of-state dark money groups have spent tens of millions of dollars trying to sell Alaskans on
ranked choice voting.
• Banned in 19 States: Dark money billionaires from the lower 48 are losing the fight for ranked choice voting all
over the country. They hope that, if they spend enough dark money here, Alaskans will keep their failed system.
• Complicated Ballots: Ranked choice ballots are a complicated mess. Ending ranked choice voting will return to
simple, One Person, One Vote elections.
• Trashed Ballots: Thousands of ballots don’t count every year. Ending ranked choice voting will ensure that
election results represent the will of all voters, not just the ones who properly fill out an overly-complex ballot.
• Manipulated Results: Due to low turnout, trashed ballots, and incorrectly filled out ballots, the results of every
election are not representative of Alaskans. This harms Alaskans, but helps candidates supported by the out-ofstate dark money.
• High Risk: Ranked choice voting has created many documented cases of election irregularities. Worse, it is
impossible to verify those questionable results by human hand count - instead we have to just trust a computer
algorithm.
• Waiting Weeks for Results: Results already take forever to collect from across Alaska. Ranked choice voting
makes that problem even worse by delaying results for weeks.
(2) Yes on 2 Brings Back Open Primaries
• Bring Back Open Primaries: Yes on 2 will *not* close Alaska’s primaries. That’s a lie. Our primaries will return to
the pre-2020 system that was open to 100% of Alaskans - including those who are not members of any party.
• Alaska’s History of Open Primaries: A nonpartisan study by the Bipartisan Policy Center rated Alaska’s elections
before the 2020 Jungle Primary system as “Open.” That’s because they were Open to 100% of Alaskan voters. A
Yes vote on 2 restores that same Open Primary system.
• Dark Money Lies: The same out-of-state money falsely claiming that Yes on 2 will close Alaska’s primaries
actually funded the nonpartisan study that rated our elections as “Open.” So, they know better. They must just
think Alaskans are dumb.
• End the Jungle Primary: Yes on 2 will end the complicated jungle primary system that resulted in 17 candidates
for governor this year and 48 candidates for Congress in 2022.
(3) Yes on 2 Restores Pre-2020 Campaign Disclosure Laws
• Dark Money is Still Flowing: The same out-of-state billionaires claiming that a Yes on 2 will cause dark money to
flow into Alaska have spent tens of millions of dollars in dark money to protect ranked choice voting.
• Defeat Ranked Choice Dark Money: Yes on 2 will defeat the largest source of dark money Alaska has ever seen
- the tens of millions of dollars spent to support ranked choice voting.
Mead Treadwell, former Lt. Governor of Alaska
Craig Campbell, former Lt. Governor of Alaska
Loren Leman, former Lt. Governor of Alaska

An Act Restoring Political Party Primaries, Ending Ranked-Choice
General Elections, and Repealing Recent Campaign Finance Laws
argumentsAgainst:
Measure 2 would ﬂood Alaska with untraceable campaign cash, take away our freedom to vote for any candidate we
choose, and allow politicians to win without a majority of the vote.
To stop Dark Money and to stop political insiders from taking away your right to vote for who you want, VOTE NO.
Alaska’s election system has three parts that together make us unique from any other state in the country:
• Dark Money disclosure laws give us the right to know who is spending in our elections and require outside
spenders to publicly disclose the true source of their funding.
• Open primaries ensure political parties do not control our primary elections and that every Alaskan has the
right to vote for whichever candidates we want.
• Ranked choice voting ensures that the winning candidate must earn the support of a majority of the voters.
Ballot Measure 2 would get rid of all three parts.
Why are the sponsors of this initiative ONLY talking about repealing ranked choice voting, with no mention of the
ﬂood of anonymous campaign cash coming our way if it passes?
Because they are trying to hide what this measure is really about:
• Ballot Measure 2 gets rid of campaign ﬁnance transparency requirements and allows secret, undisclosed
spending in Alaska’s elections.
• Ballot Measure 2 also gives political party bosses the right to deny unafﬁliated voters the ability to vote in
primary elections. 60%+ of Alaskan voters are unafﬁliated.
Voting No protects voter freedom:
• Voting No says NO to Outside Billionaires buying our elections with no accountability.
• Voting No afﬁrms that Alaskans have the right to know who is spending in our elections.
• Voting No protects every Alaskans’ freedom to vote in every election.
A few questions to consider before you vote:
• Do you think we should have LESS transparency in our elections?
• Do you think names of those spending money in Alaska’s elections should be kept SECRET?
• Do you think we should give more power and inﬂuence to political party insiders and their outside billionaire
donors?
• Do you think we should allow political parties to ban 60%+ of Alaskans from voting in primary elections just
because they prefer not to join a party?
If your answers to any of these questions is NO, you should vote NO on Ballot Measure 2.
This is the third time in six years that Alaskans are being asked to vote on our election system. Special interest
groups and political party insiders are demanding we waste more time and money on this costly repeat ballot
measure so that they can take power away from the voters and back for themselves.
This issue is not Democrats vs. Republicans. It is Alaskans vs. Outside Billionaires and political insiders.
Vote No on Measure 2 to stop Dark Money and protect Alaskans’ independence.
Nicole Borromeo, President, ANCSA Regional Association
Sen. Cathy Giessel, Senate Majority Leader (R)
Joelle Hall, President, Alaska AFL-CIO

voterGuide.summary:
Alaska statute has four requirements a person must meet before they can vote. First, the person must
be a citizen of the United States. Second, the person must be at least 18 years of age or older. Third,
the person must be a resident of Alaska and the applicable state house district for 30 days before the
election. And fourth, the person must have registered to vote in Alaska and cannot be registered to
vote in another jurisdiction. This Act would reword that statute so that it says only a person who meets
all four requirements may vote. This Act would not change the requirements or qualifications to vote.

argumentsFor:
By Sponsors John Coghill, Mike Chenault, and Josh Revak
What is Ballot Measure 25USCV?
Ballot Measure 25USCV is a citizens’ initiative that would add clarity to Alaska law by stating that only
United States citizens may be qualified voters in Alaska elections.
Current law says citizens may vote, but it does not specifically state that only citizens may vote. This
measure closes that gap and makes Alaska law unmistakably clear.
It does not change who is a U.S. citizen or affect federal immigration law. It clarifies Alaska election law
so it reflects what most voters already understand: when Alaskans cast ballots for local, state, or federal
offices, they are participating in a uniquely American act of self-government reserved for citizens.
What will Ballot Measure 25USCV do?
If approved, this measure will write into law that voter qualification in Alaska is limited to
U.S. citizens, while keeping existing protections against discrimination on the basis of race, gender,
religion, or disability.
The initiative does not change registration procedures for eligible citizens. It clarifies that non-citizens,
even if lawfully present, may not register or vote in state or local elections.
Ballot Measure 25USCV also helps ensure that Alaska’s election system remains straightforward and
easier to run. Clear standards reduce confusion at the Division of Elections, the DMV, and other agencies
that help register voters, and they make it less likely that ineligible individuals will be accidentally added to
the rolls.
What will voting YES on Ballot Measure 25USCV do?
A YES vote will affirm that Alaskans want to keep voting a core right and responsibility of citizenship.
Around the country, a growing number of cities have begun allowing certain non-citizens to vote in local
elections, creating confusion and controversy about who should participate in choosing community leaders
and passing laws. By passing 25USCV, Alaska will make clear that it is not going down that path.
Voting YES will also give clearer guidance to election officials and potential voters. When the rule is simple
— you must be a U.S. citizen to vote — people are less likely to make honest mistakes, and the state is
better able to maintain accurate voter lists.
Vote YES to Protect the Integrity of Alaska’s Elections
Alaskans are proud of a tradition of civic participation, close-knit communities, and competitive elections
decided by small margins. Public confidence that every legal vote counts — and that only legal votes
count — is essential.
Ballot Measure 25USCV strengthens that confidence by confirming in law that Alaska elections are for
U.S. citizens, while leaving intact all of the ways eligible Alaskans can register and vote.
This initiative also honors the path of legal immigration and citizenship. It supports immigrants who work
hard to become U.S. citizens and then fully earn the right to vote.
John Coghill Jr., Former Senator
Charles M. Chenault, Former Speaker of the House
Joshua C. Revak, Former Alaska State Senator

An Act Addressing Voter Qualification

measureRecords.whatItDoes:
AN INITIATIVE TO:
REQUIRE THAT ONLY UNITED STATES CITIZENS MAY BE QUALIFIED VOTERS IN
ALASKA ELECTIONS.
A BILL BY INITIATIVE
For an Act Entitled
“An Act requiring that only United States citizens may be qualified to vote in Alaska elections”
BE IT ENACTED BY THE PEOPLE OF THE STATE OF ALASKA:
*Section 1.
